strengths: Addresses a practical problem of inference-time multi-preference alignment without additional fine-tuning
Provides theoretical justification through propositions connecting aligned diffusion to weighted reward combinations
Comprehensive experiments across multiple reward functions (ImageReward, VILA, PickScore) with extensive qualitative visualizations
Computationally efficient approach compared to retraining models for different preference configurations
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution (blending multiple objectives) is straightforward and represents incremental extension of existing RL fine-tuning methods for diffusion models
Weak experimental baselines: Comparisons primarily against simple methods (RS, CoDe, RGG); missing comparisons with recent multi-objective alignment approaches and stronger alternatives
No user studies: Claims about alignment quality rely solely on reward scores and visual inspection, without human evaluation critical for validating preference alignment

Questionable theoretical soundness: Jensen gap approximation (Eq. 8) lacks formal justification; Lemma 1 bounds are loose with unclear practical utility; assumption that fine-tuning Eq. (4) solves Eq. (3) is not rigorously justified
Incomplete evaluation: Small test set (25 prompts), only on dated Stable Diffusion v1.5, missing error bars/significance tests, DB-KLA has limited baseline comparisons
Scalability issues: Requires m separately pre-trained reward-aligned models; linear combination assumption (Eq. 3) may be too restrictive for complex preference trade-offs
Clarity problems: Core contribution unclear; overclaimed results ('consistently outperforms'); missing ablations on critical design choices; limited analysis of failure modes
Missing key comparisons: No comparison with simpler alternatives (ensemble methods, training single model for multiple objectives, direct preference optimization) or recent related work
Reproducibility concerns: Insufficient implementation details, hyperparameter choices not justified, no link to code, missing computational cost analysis

strengths: Novel problem formulation addressing practical limitations of existing RL fine-tuning: enabling inference-time multi-preference alignment without additional fine-tuning
Solid theoretical contributions with rigorous derivations of closed-form solutions (Proposition 1, Lemmas 1-3) and principled approximation error bounds
Elegant technical solution: blending backward diffusion processes is a clever insight that enables flexible preference composition with minimal computational overhead

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple reward functions, quantitative/qualitative results, systematic baseline comparisons, and Pareto-frontier analysis demonstrating clear performance benefits
Strong empirical validation: DB-MPA consistently outperforms baselines (RS, CoDe, RGG) with improvements of 1.67-2.43× across different reward metrics
Effective smooth preference control demonstrated: figures show smooth transitions between user-specified preferences without discrete jumps
Good reproducibility: pseudo-code, detailed hyperparameters, extensive appendices enable reproduction
Clear presentation and strong motivation for the problem throughout the paper
weaknesses: Limited generalization scope: all experiments on single model (Stable Diffusion v1.5); no validation on other architectures (DALL-E 3, Flux) limits claims about general framework applicability
Memory overhead not thoroughly analyzed: method requires maintaining m fine-tuned models in memory during inference; practical memory costs not quantified or compared to alternative approaches
Missing human evaluation: despite focusing on user preferences, evaluation relies entirely on learned reward models without human studies; weakens claims about actual user preference alignment
Incomplete baseline comparisons: MORL presented as oracle rather than direct competitor; no comparison with other recent multi-objective RL methods for diffusion models
Empirical validation of approximation bounds lacking: Lemma 1 provides error bounds but tightness not validated empirically; sensitivity to assumption violations not explored
Linear reward combination assumption not justified: paper assumes linear combinations optimal without exploring non-linear alternatives or justifying this design choice
Hyperparameter selection guidance incomplete: how to select λ in practice not clearly addressed; limited analysis of sensitivity to other hyperparameters
Limited failure case analysis: while some failures shown in Figure 5, comprehensive analysis of failure modes and method limitations absent

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing the inflexibility of standard RL fine-tuning for diffusion models when users need to specify different preferences at inference time
Principled theoretical framework with rigorous SDE decomposition (Proposition 1) and approximation analysis (Lemmas 1-3) that avoids approximating individual fine-tuned models
Computationally efficient lightweight variant (DB-MPA-LS) that maintains performance while reducing inference cost through clever random sampling
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple datasets, reward functions, baselines, and ablation studies showing substantial improvements over competing methods
Strong empirical results achieving near-oracle performance (individually fine-tuned models) while maintaining original inference cost and demonstrating clear visual improvements
weaknesses: Critical treatment of training cost overhead—requires pre-training and fine-tuning m separate models, which is substantial but largely glossed over; no comparison to single-model weighted reward training

Significant gap between theory and practice: Proposition 1 claims exactness but all experiments use Jensen approximation; no empirical validation of approximation quality or analysis of bound tightness
Missing user studies validating that generated outputs actually match user-specified preferences; all evaluation uses automated metrics, which may not correlate with human preference satisfaction

Incomplete baseline comparisons: MORL used only as oracle rather than actual competing method; missing comparisons to weighted reward training and other multi-objective inference-time guidance methods
Limited scope and generalizability—only evaluated on text-to-image diffusion; unclear applicability to other generative models or diffusion settings; SDXL results relegated to appendix

Insufficient analysis of scalability, failure modes, and approximation robustness—no exploration of behavior with many rewards (m>>4), sensitivity to diffusion steps T, or which reward combinations blend well

Technical gaps: conditions for Eq. (8) approximation validity unclear; Proposition 2 extension to arbitrary m claimed straightforward without justification; reversibility assumptions of fine-tuned models not validated
Incremental core novelty—while technically sound, the basic insight that SDE backward processes can be blended is relatively straightforward once decomposition is observed

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: Enables inference-time multi-preference alignment without fine-tuning, addressing a genuine limitation of existing RL fine-tuning approaches
Strong theoretical foundation: Propositions 1-2 rigorously characterize alignment in the backward diffusion process with well-derived approximation error bounds (Lemmas 1-2)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets (ShortDrawBench, GenEval, SDXL), diverse metrics, appropriate baseline comparisons, and extensive ablations across preference weights, reward counts, and conflicting objectives
Practical efficiency: DB-MPA-LS variant achieves 2x inference speedup while maintaining near-DB-MPA performance through clever LoRA sampling approximation
Scalability demonstration: Validated on both Stable Diffusion v1.5 and SDXL models showing generalization across scales
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-structured paper with clear problem formulation, algorithmic descriptions, pseudo-code, and code released on GitHub
Effective visualization of preference transitions: Qualitative results clearly demonstrate smooth control over multiple objectives without retraining
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons: MORL treated only as oracle baseline; missing comparisons to recent multi-objective optimization methods and other inference-time alignment approaches
Incomplete approximation analysis: Jensen gap approximation impact is not thoroughly empirically analyzed; assumptions on R(x) bounds appear somewhat arbitrary and lack detailed justification
Insufficient characterization of conflicting objectives: Limited systematic study of performance degradation as objectives become increasingly contradictory; missing explicit failure mode analysis
Lack of human evaluation: Relies entirely on automated metrics (ImageReward, VILA, PickScore) without human studies to validate alignment quality, particularly important for aesthetic preferences
Incomplete scalability analysis: Experiments only show up to m=4 rewards; missing systematic study of computational and quality limits as number of objectives increases
Limited sensitivity analysis: While smooth control is demonstrated, deeper analysis of weight selection sensitivity is missing; no practical guidance for choosing preference weights
Insufficient discussion of method limits: Assumptions underlying Proposition 1 (closed-form decomposition) not extensively discussed; scope and validity not clearly characterized
Dense notation in places: Multiple levels of superscripts and subscripts make some equations difficult to parse; could benefit from simplified presentation in key results
